What is deliberately not trained One variable of the 34 configured. sea_surface_salinity is configured, its provider works, and it will not be trained — the YAML block says so, with the numbers, so that nobody retrains it in the belief that it was an oversight. Point salinity barely moves day to day, which makes persistence near-unbeatable; retraining reproduces those numbers rather than better ones. The covariates are not the problem, the target's own persistence is. Each such variable still gets a metric page at /dashboard/<variable> that renders its history and correctly omits the forecast section, with the command to train it. A page that implied a working forecast where none passed the bar would be worse than no page at all. Next: the same engine rendered as a global map .

label: The forecast map
title: The same engine, drawn as a map
text: Forecasting engine The same engine, drawn as a map A point forecast answers "what happens here". A field answers "where is something about to happen", which is a different and usually more useful question. The forecast map runs the identical pipeline over a global grid and renders the result as a raster layer on the map — the same models, the same features, the same code path, with the network replaced by an in-memory slice. Two modes, and only one of them is interesting Mode What it draws Why Absolute The predicted field itself. Reads like the observation layer it forecasts. Familiar, and largely redundant. Change Forecast minus the latest observation. The informative one. At +7 days the absolute field looks almost exactly like today's, so the signal is entirely in the difference. The change ramp is diverging and must stay symmetric around zero, or "no change" drifts off the neutral colour and the map starts implying a trend that is not there. The grid path is the point path This is the design decision the whole feature rests on. The gridded builder does not have its own feature engineering. Its history stack exposes a per-cell slice in exactly the shape the point path's fetcher returns, and the cell loop then calls the same build → clean → featurise chain that a single-point forecast calls. Why there is deliberately no grid-native feature builder A vectorised, grid-aware reimplementation of the feature engineering would be much faster — and it is exactly how train/serve skew gets in. The model was fitted on features produced by one code path; if the map produces them by another, the two will agree at first and drift apart at the first change to either. A 40,000-cell loop is precisely where the temptation to write one is strongest, so the test that compares both paths cell-for-cell on identical synthetic inputs is what makes optimising the loop safe to attempt at all. They agree to 1e-6. The fetch is inverted This is a third access pattern the platform did not previously have. The downloader asks for one bounded area over many timesteps; the map tiles ask for the whole globe at one timestep. A gridded forecast needs the whole globe over many timesteps , which is the expensive corner of that space. Copernicus publishes two zarr services with opposite chunking, and picking the wrong one turns a ten-second read into hours. The geo-series service stores one global timestep per chunk, which is right here; the time-series service would touch every spatial chunk on the planet. Striding to the output resolution happens while the array is still lazy, which is not an optimisation but a requirement: a global 0.083° float64 field is about 70 MB per timestep per variable, so 45 timesteps of two variables at full resolution is over 6 GB. What it costs, and what does not change it Stage Cost Scales with output resolution? Fetch ~1080 whole-globe reads, ~35 min No Cell loop ~15 min at 1° (22 ms/cell × ~42,000 cells) Yes The consequence is worth internalising before anyone tunes it: cost is dominated by the fetch, and the fetch does not care about the output resolution. Passing --resolution 4.0 speeds up the loop and nothing else. Reads are disk-cached for six hours and shared across every variable drawing on the same dataset, so building several variables together is far cheaper than building them one at a time. A 40× cheaper option was measured and deliberately not taken Daily Copernicus products exist and would cut the fetch dramatically. Adopting them would also make the dataframe builder's inner join collapse hourly wind onto a daily axis — turning wind speed from a 24-hour mean into one instantaneous value, silently, for every model that uses it as a covariate. That has to be solved first. Some variables can never be gridded Open-Meteo is a point API capped at 900 points, so air_temperature — itself a trained variable, and a covariate of sea surface temperature — has no global field and never will through this route. The builder states this rather than absorbing it: An ungriddable target is skipped before paying for any fetch, with the reason recorded. An ungriddable covariate is recorded in the grid file's missing_covariates attribute and surfaced in the layer's attribution — because LightGBM routes an absent feature down its missing-value branch without complaint, and the resulting map would otherwise look exactly as confident as a complete one. The legend lives in the data file Display bounds and the change scale are computed at build time as robust percentiles rounded outward, and stored as attributes on the grid itself. The tile renderer and the frontend legend both read them from there, so they cannot disagree about what a colour means — a legend that describes a different scale than the pixels is a quietly wrong map, not a cosmetic bug. Sea surface temperature is colour-matched to the existing observation layer, because comparing the forecast against observed SST is the first thing anyone does with it. Layers appear without a frontend edit A forecast layer exists only where a model is trained and its grid has been built, which is not knowable at build time. So these layers are not in the static layer registry: the map fetches the forecast tile catalog at runtime and registers whatever it finds. A newly built grid becomes a map layer with no code change. python scripts/build_forecast_grid.py --variable chlorophyll_a --resolution 1.0 Grids are rebuilt by a twice-daily scheduled job that skips anything already fresh, and save_grid writes only after a successful build — so a failed rebuild leaves the previous grid in place rather than blanking the layer. The build must run off the event loop, and a timing test would not catch it Everything past the fetch — the cell loop, inference, assembly — is roughly 15 minutes of CPU with no await in it, and the scheduler starts it at boot. Awaited inline, it stalls every request on the process for that entire window, which presents as an API that mysteriously dies twice a day rather than as an error. The test asserts on the thread the work runs on, not on how long it takes, because the synthetic stack used in tests builds in milliseconds — any timing-based check would pass happily with the work back on the event loop. Forecast particles are a second, separate case Everything above is the scalar grid — one raster, one legend, one colour per cell. A forecast of a moving field (wind, currents) is drawn a different way entirely: as forecast particles, the same GPU particle layer the live wind and currents already use, built once both a variable's eastward and northward components are trained and gridded. It registers at runtime exactly like the scalar layers do, from a separate vector catalog endpoint, so a newly-trained pair becomes a map layer with no frontend edit either. These land in the stackable Wind & Currents group, not the exclusive one the scalar forecasts use — deliberately, because the point of a forecast particle layer is running it alongside its live counterpart and watching where the two disagree, which only works if both can be on screen at once. Every forecast pair used to be drawn as currents, and it looked fine Before the wind components were trained, the vector layer had only ever drawn currents, so every forecast pair — including an early wind forecast — inherited the currents ramp and speed scale. An 8 m/s wind field on a ramp whose domain tops out at 2 m/s renders as one flat top colour, and at the currents speed scale it advects roughly 265 px/s. Both failures animate convincingly: a wrong legend and a wrong pace each look exactly like a working layer, which is the same hazard the scalar grids solve with hatching for a different kind of wrongness. The fix was a lookup keyed on the pair itself, so a forecast field is always drawn with its own live layer's identity — never an unrelated one's. Direction still has to be handled as an angle end to end (see Directions & colour ) — which is exactly why these are forecast components rather than a forecast bearing: a model trained on the raw compass change treats a five-degree veer across north as a 355° swing, an error these particle layers were built to avoid inheriting.

label: Overview
title: Overview
text: Machine learning Overview: what this section is Maris AI runs two machine learning models over open ocean data: one that forecasts harmful algal blooms three to seven days ahead, and one that maps where five commercially important fish species are likely to be. These pages explain both of them completely — the problem, every input variable, how the data was fetched, every feature we engineered, the algorithms, the validation, and the measured results, including the parts that did not work. Who this is written for A student who has finished an introductory machine learning course, or an engineer in their first job who has trained a model on a Kaggle CSV but never on data that came out of the ocean. You need to know what a train/test split is. You do not need to know what a mixed layer depth is, what the Okubo–Weiss parameter measures, or why a random K-fold split is a catastrophe on satellite data. All of that gets explained where it first comes up. Ocean-science jargon appears in grey Jargon buster boxes. Machine learning concepts that go beyond a first course — probability calibration, PR-AUC, spatial block cross-validation, target-group background sampling — get their own sections rather than a passing mention. A note on honesty Every number in these docs is a real measurement from a real run in this repository, reproducible with the commands in the last chapter. Where a model performs badly, the bad number is printed. Two of the most useful sections describe results that got worse after we fixed a bug — because the original higher number was measuring the wrong thing. The two problems in one paragraph each Problem A — harmful algal bloom (HAB) early warning. Certain phytoplankton, given enough nutrients and the right water conditions, multiply explosively. Some of those blooms strip the water of oxygen and kill fish; some produce toxins that close beaches and shellfish beds. We forecast chlorophyll concentration three, five and seven days ahead across the Arabian Sea, and declare a bloom wherever the forecast crosses a threshold calibrated to that specific grid cell in that specific season. Problem B — fish habitat / Potential Fishing Zone (PFZ). India's national ocean service (INCOIS) publishes advisories telling fishing crews where to go, based largely on hand-tuned sea-surface-temperature front detection. We learn the same kind of map from data: given ocean conditions at a location and time, how suitable is it for yellowfin tuna, skipjack tuna, bigeye tuna, Indian mackerel, or oil sardine. The shape of the code Both problems sit on one shared foundation, called the Marine Data Fusion Layer . Data ingestion, regridding, the feature store, the geometry and time feature libraries, and the entire validation harness are written once and imported by both. Only the labels and the problem-specific derived features differ. That is not tidiness for its own sake: it is the guarantee that "sea surface temperature gradient" means exactly the same computation in both models. Directory What lives there marine_ml/ The shared spine — configuration, data sources, fusion/regridding, the feature store, geometry and temporal feature libraries, splitters and metrics. hab_early_warning/src/ Problem A only — bloom labelling, HAB-specific features, the training loop for three forecast horizons. fish_habitat_prediction/src/ Problem B only — presence/background labelling, habitat features, the three model tiers and their ensemble. scripts/ Populating the raw data zone, and exporting prediction grids for the web app to serve. tests/ Tests that the pipeline cannot cheat — see the validation chapter. reports/ Every number quoted in these docs: per-fold scores, held-out metrics, SHAP rankings, calibration curves. What this is not The models here are what a serious pipeline looks like at the "Tier 1 and Tier 2" stage: gradient-boosted trees, regularised linear baselines, and careful validation. There is no ConvLSTM, no vision transformer, no GPU. That is deliberate and explained in the limitations chapter . Deep spatio-temporal models are worth building on top of a proven pipeline; they are a very expensive way to find out that your cross-validation was leaking. Suggested reading order Straight through. But if you are short on time and want the parts that generalise beyond this project, read Validation & leakage and Metrics, explained — those two chapters contain the mistakes that are easiest to make and hardest to notice in any applied ML project, not just this one.

label: ML primer
title: A primer
text: Machine learning A primer: ML vocabulary, in ocean terms If you already know what supervised learning, features, labels, class imbalance and overfitting are, skip to the next chapter. This one maps the standard vocabulary onto what the ocean data actually looks like, so the rest of the docs can move fast. Supervised learning, and what a "row" is here Both of our models are supervised classifiers : you hand the model a table where each row describes one situation, and one column is the answer you want it to learn to predict. The model learns a function from the other columns (the features ) to the answer (the label ). The interesting part of applied ML is almost never the classifier — it is deciding what a row is , and where the label comes from. Problem A (HAB) Problem B (habitat) One row is… one 0.25° grid cell on one calendar day one observation point — a place and date where a fish was recorded, or where the survey recorded something else The label is… will chlorophyll here exceed this cell's seasonal bloom threshold in 3 / 5 / 7 days? (1 or 0) was this species present here? (1) or is this a background point? (0) Number of rows ≈ 3.84 million 2,787 Number of features 136 40 Where the label comes from the data itself — a percentile of modelled chlorophyll (a "weak" label) OBIS, a global database of species occurrence records The two problems could not be more different in shape: millions of rows of a regular grid versus a few thousand scattered points. Almost every design decision downstream follows from that difference. Features, and why "feature engineering" matters so much here A feature is any number you compute from what you know, and hand to the model as input. The raw ocean data gives us temperature, salinity, chlorophyll, currents and so on — but handed to a model raw, those numbers answer the wrong question. A model told only "the temperature here is 28.4 °C" has no way to know whether that is unusually warm for this place, in this season , or whether it has been climbing for a fortnight. So most of the work is turning raw fields into features that encode the physics and the ecology: Anomalies — how far today's value is from this cell's normal value for this month. Lags — what the value was 3, 7, 14 and 30 days ago. Rolling statistics — the average and variability over the past week or month. Spatial derivatives — how sharply temperature changes across space (that's a "front", and fish gather at them). Interactions — warm water over a shallow mixed layer traps a bloom near the surface; neither term alone says that. The feature engineering chapter works through every one of them. Train, validation, test — and why random splitting is banned here Standard practice: hold out part of your data, train on the rest, and measure on what you held out. The universal beginner default is to shuffle the rows and take a random 20%. On this data that is not a small inaccuracy, it is meaningless. Ocean fields are autocorrelated — a fancy word for "today looks almost exactly like yesterday, and this pixel looks almost exactly like the pixel next to it". If you shuffle randomly, a grid cell's Tuesday lands in training and its Wednesday lands in test. The model does not have to learn any oceanography to score beautifully; it just has to recognise near-duplicates of rows it already saw. The single most important idea in these docs A validation score is not a property of a model. It is a property of a model and the way you split the data. Change the split and the same model reports a wildly different number. Everywhere in this project you will see scores that look worse than a random split would have given — that gap is the honest part. So we use two structured splits instead, one per problem: Rolling-origin (time series) splits for the bloom forecast. Train on the past, test on the future, and throw away a few days in between. Chapter: Validation & leakage . Spatial block splits for the habitat model. Hold out whole 3° squares of ocean, so the test points are physically far from any training point. Leakage Leakage is when information that would not be available at prediction time sneaks into training. It is the reason a model can look excellent in a notebook and be useless in production, and it is far easier to introduce than to detect — because its only symptom is a score that looks good . Three ways it happens on time-series ocean data, all of which we guard against: A "lag" feature that reads forwards. One misplaced sign in a shift() and your model is told tomorrow's chlorophyll while predicting tomorrow's bloom. A rolling window that includes the current timestep. A "past 7 days" average that quietly includes today. A statistic fitted on all the data. This one is subtle and it bit us: our bloom labels are defined by a percentile threshold. Compute that percentile over the whole record, including the test years, and you have leaked the future into the definition of the target itself. The codebase handles this structurally rather than by being careful: every "fit-then-apply" pair is split into two separate functions, so fitting on the wrong rows requires actively passing the wrong table. # Correct by construction — you have to name the training rows. thresholds = fit_bloom_thresholds(train_frame) # fit: training only frame = apply_bloom_thresholds(frame, thresholds) # apply: everywhere Class imbalance Blooms are rare. In our held-out year about 7.4% of grid-cell-days are labelled as blooms. A model that predicts "no bloom" every single time is 92.6% accurate and completely worthless. Two consequences run through the whole project: Accuracy is never reported. We use PR-AUC, TSS and Brier score instead — all explained in Metrics, explained . The training loss is reweighted ( class_weight="balanced" ), so a missed bloom costs the model much more than a false alarm. This keeps the rare class learnable — but it distorts the predicted probabilities, which is why we then have to calibrate them. Gradient-boosted trees, in sixty seconds Both problems' best model is LightGBM , a gradient-boosting library. The idea: train a small decision tree; look at where it was wrong; train a second small tree to predict those errors; add it to the first; repeat a few hundred times. Each tree is weak, the sum is strong. Why it suits this data specifically: It handles missing values natively — and our data is full of them, because clouds, satellite swath gaps and land all produce holes. It captures thresholds and interactions automatically. Ecology is full of "below 200 m depth everything changes" effects that a linear model cannot express. It does not need features scaled to the same range, so depth in metres and chlorophyll in mg/m³ can sit side by side. It stays explainable through SHAP — a method that attributes each individual prediction to the features that drove it, so the product can say why a cell is flagged, not just that it is. prediction = tree₁(x) + tree₂(x) + … + tree₅₀₀(x) → sigmoid → probability Each tree is depth-limited (max_depth 5–6 here) so no single tree can memorise the training set. The learning rate (0.05) shrinks each tree's contribution, which is what makes the sum stable. What "a good result" looks like on this data Coming from tutorial datasets, the scores in these docs may look low. A held-out PR-AUC of 0.36 for the seven-day bloom forecast is not a failing grade — it is a real forecast of a rare, chaotic biological event a week into the future, measured on water and time the model never saw, against a baseline that scores 0.31. Whether that is useful is a separate question from whether it is good, and we answer it with false-alarm rates rather than with AUCs.

label: The two problems
title: The two problem statements
text: Machine learning The two problem statements Why harmful algal blooms and fishing zones specifically — out of everything you could model in an ocean — and what exactly each model is being asked to output. This chapter is the "why", the rest of the section is the "how". Why these two Both problems share three properties that make them worth building, and that a lot of ocean ML ideas fail: There is a real decision at the other end. A bloom forecast changes whether a coastal agency issues an advisory. A habitat map changes where a boat spends its fuel. Neither is a metric with no consumer. The labels exist without a bespoke field campaign. Chlorophyll comes from an open reanalysis product; species occurrences come from OBIS, an open global database. We could not have modelled, say, illegal fishing or plastic transport at this cost. There is an operational incumbent to be measured against. India's INCOIS already publishes PFZ advisories and Algal Bloom Information Service bulletins. That means "is this actually better than what exists" is a question with a meaning, even where we cannot yet run the comparison. Problem A — harmful algal bloom early warning Jargon buster — what a harmful algal bloom is Phytoplankton are microscopic plants drifting in the sunlit surface layer of the ocean. Give them light plus a sudden supply of nutrients (nitrate, phosphate, silicate) and their population can multiply many times over within days — a bloom . Blooms are the base of the marine food web and mostly a good thing. A harmful algal bloom is one where either (a) the species involved produces a toxin that accumulates in shellfish and sickens people, or (b) the bloom is so dense that when it dies and decomposes it consumes the oxygen in the water and suffocates everything else — a fish kill. Chlorophyll-a is the green pigment phytoplankton use for photosynthesis. Its concentration (mg per cubic metre) is the standard proxy for how much phytoplankton is present, and it is what satellites and ocean models can actually measure at scale. The forecast, precisely stated For each 0.25° cell of the Arabian Sea on each day t , output the probability that chlorophyll at that same cell on day t+3 , t+5 and t+7 will exceed that cell's bloom threshold for that monsoon season. Three separate models, one per horizon. Forecast-then-threshold, not straight classification The obvious framing is "train a binary classifier on bloom / no bloom". We deliberately did not. Instead the target is defined by forecasting the underlying continuous quantity and comparing it to a locally calibrated threshold. Three things that buys: A meaningful risk score. The output is a trajectory of chlorophyll plus a distance above the local normal, not an opaque yes/no. A retunable threshold. A different region, season, or agency risk appetite means a different threshold — and none of that requires retraining the model. Honesty about what the label is. A fixed global cutoff is not physically meaningful: 1 mg/m³ of chlorophyll is an extreme anomaly in the open Arabian Sea and an ordinary Tuesday in a coastal upwelling zone. The threshold has to be local. Read this before quoting any HAB number What we train on is a weak label . "Modelled chlorophyll above this cell's seasonal 90th percentile" is a proxy for a bloom. It is not a verified bloom, and it says nothing at all about toxicity. Verified labels would need in-situ cell counts and toxin assays — HABSOS, NCCOS, HAEDAT, or INCOIS advisories — and none of those is openly queryable for this coastline. One direct consequence: our positive class rate is around 9.7% in training, not the "low single digits" real blooms would give. That is arithmetic, not oceanography — a 90th-percentile threshold produces ~10% positives by construction. Region and window Setting Value Why Region Arabian Sea — 68–78°E, 6–23°N A bounded box. Daily fields over a wide region are prohibitively expensive to fetch, so the region gives. Cadence Daily Non-negotiable: the product is a t+3/t+5/t+7 day forecast. Window 2016-01-01 → 2021-12-31 Six years puts five southwest-monsoon bloom seasons in the training period. An earlier two-year window put in exactly one, and the model collapsed — see below. Grid 0.25° (≈ 28 km) Matches the biogeochemistry product's native resolution — the coarsest input. The window was measured, not chosen The first version of this model ran on 2020–2021. It scored well until we moved the validation slice out of training, at which point the seven-day model dropped to ROC-AUC 0.53 — literally chance. The cause was not tuning: monthly mean chlorophyll in the 2021 southwest monsoon ran ~40% higher than 2020's (August: 0.229 vs 0.164 mg/m³), so the model was being asked about an ocean regime it had never seen. Extending to six years fixed it outright. The bloom rate across train / validation / test went from 10.4% → 16.5% → 21.2% (drifting badly) to 10.2% → 9.4% → 7.6% (flat), and t+7 ROC-AUC went from 0.53 to 0.841. More years beat more features , because no covariate helps a model that has never seen the regime it is being asked about. Problem B — fish habitat / Potential Fishing Zone Jargon buster — PFZ and SDM A Potential Fishing Zone advisory is a map published to fishing crews showing where fish are likely to aggregate. INCOIS issues these for the Indian coast; at heart the operational method is a hand-tuned detector for sea-surface-temperature fronts — boundaries where warm and cold water meet. Fronts concentrate nutrients and small prey, so predators concentrate there too. A species distribution model (SDM) is the ecology term for what we are building: a model of the relationship between where a species has been observed and the environmental conditions there, used to map suitability everywhere else. The SDM literature has its own vocabulary and its own metrics, and we follow it rather than generic ML convention — that is why you will see the Boyce index and TSS instead of F1. The prediction, precisely stated For a given species, location, month and set of ocean conditions, output a habitat suitability score between 0 and 1. Five species are modelled in one shared model, with the species itself as an input feature: Key Scientific name Common name yellowfin_tuna Thunnus albacares Yellowfin tuna skipjack_tuna Katsuwonus pelamis Skipjack tuna bigeye_tuna Thunnus obesus Bigeye tuna indian_mackerel Rastrelliger kanagurta Indian mackerel oil_sardine Sardinella longiceps Oil sardine Commercially significant species of the Indian EEZ with enough OBIS occurrence records in the region to model. Record counts were checked against the OBIS API before the list was fixed, not assumed. Stacking all five into one table rather than training five separate models is deliberate: species with few records borrow strength from the shared environmental response. It is the tabular equivalent of a shared encoder with per-species output heads. The hard part is not the classifier OBIS is presence-only . There is no record anywhere in it that says "we looked here and found nothing". So the negative class has to be manufactured, and how you manufacture it decides what the model learns. Get it wrong and you produce a beautiful map of where marine biologists work. The habitat chapter covers the fix — target-group background sampling — in full, because it matters more to the credibility of this model than every hyperparameter combined. Region and window Setting Value Why Region North Indian Ocean — 55–95°E, 5°S–25°N Occurrence-record density collapses outside it. A narrow box returns single-digit records for most target species; this one returns 280–400 for the tunas. Cadence Monthly Occurrence records carry imprecise dates. Sampling daily fields against them would be false precision — and monthly means make a wide region affordable. Window 2000-01-01 → 2013-12-31 Set by label availability, not by what Copernicus can serve. Target-species records in this region effectively stop after 2014. Grid 0.25° The same shared grid as Problem A, so a feature means the same thing in both. Two different windows, one shared codebase The two problems cover different boxes over different years at different cadences. That is not a failure of the shared design — the guarantee the shared layer makes is that a feature means the same thing in both , not that both cover the same water. Both profiles run through identical ingestion, fusion and feature code. What we deliberately did not build HAB Stage 2 — toxicity classification. Deciding whether a bloom is harmful needs in-situ genus and toxin data. None is openly queryable for this coastline, so the interface carries a label_strength field and the classifier is left unimplemented rather than faked on data that does not exist. Fishing-effort data as a label. Global Fishing Watch data is registered in the source inventory but not ingested. Vessel positions must stay a covariate and an external validation signal, never a target — "fish are where boats are, and boats are where fish are" is a circular model that would score well and mean nothing.

label: Data & variables
title: Every variable, and how we fetched it
text: Machine learning Every variable, and how we fetched it Five data sources: seventeen gridded ocean-state variables, a seafloor relief grid, species occurrence records — and a set of fetch decisions that are the difference between a pipeline that runs in minutes and one that never finishes. This chapter lists every input and explains what each one physically means. The four sources Source What it gives us Access Native resolution Copernicus Marine — physics reanalysis Temperature, salinity, currents, sea surface height, mixed layer depth cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m 1/12° (≈ 9 km), daily & monthly Copernicus Marine — biogeochemistry Chlorophyll, nutrients, oxygen, primary production cmems_mod_glo_bgc_my_0.25deg_P1D-m 1/4° (≈ 28 km), daily & monthly Copernicus Marine — L4 scatterometer wind Wind stress, stress curl, 10 m winds cmems_obs-wind_glo_phy_my_l4_0.125deg_PT1H 0.125°, hourly NOAA ERDDAP (ETOPO / GEBCO-class relief) Seafloor depth and elevation → slope, distance to coast etopo180 griddap endpoint ≈ 15 arc-seconds, static OBIS Species occurrence records (Problem B labels + background pool) api.obis.org/v3/occurrence Point records Jargon buster — reanalysis vs. near-real-time A reanalysis is a physics model of the ocean, run backwards over history with every observation available at the time assimilated into it. It produces a gap-free, physically consistent record of the past, reprocessed as one consistent product. That is what training needs. The near-real-time products the Maris AI map page uses are the opposite trade: fast and current, but only reaching back a couple of years and without the same consistency. The _my_ in the dataset IDs above stands for "multi-year" — it is the reanalysis edition, and it is why the ML pipeline and the live map read from different products. Physical ocean variables Six variables from the physics reanalysis, all taken at the surface layer (~0.49 m depth). thetao °C — sea water potential temperature At the surface layer this is sea surface temperature. It sets metabolic rates for everything living in the water, defines fronts, and is the single most-used field in marine ecology. so PSU — practical salinity How salty the water is. Distinguishes water masses: river-influenced coastal water, high-salinity Arabian Sea water, and monsoon-freshened surface layers are different habitats. uo m/s — eastward current velocity The east–west component of surface current. Combined with vo it gives speed, vorticity and the eddy diagnostics. vo m/s — northward current velocity The north–south component. Its sign near a coast also acts as a crude upwelling proxy when observed wind stress is unavailable. zos m — sea surface height above geoid Where the sea surface bulges up or dips down. Highs and lows are the signature of eddies and of the large-scale circulation, and this turned out to be one of the habitat model's strongest predictors. mlotst m — mixed layer thickness How deep the surface layer is that wind and waves keep well stirred. A shallow mixed layer traps phytoplankton in the sunlight (bloom-friendly); a deep one mixes them down into the dark. Biogeochemical variables Six variables from the biogeochemistry reanalysis. This is model biogeochemistry, not satellite ocean colour, and that is a deliberate choice for the HAB problem: it is not cloud-limited, so it gives continuous daily coverage where satellite chlorophyll has holes — and the southwest monsoon, precisely when blooms happen, is exactly when the Arabian Sea is cloudiest. chl mg/m³ — chlorophyll-a concentration The quantity Problem A forecasts, and the proxy for how much phytoplankton is in the water. Spans orders of magnitude, so it is usually handled in log space. no3 mmol/m³ — nitrate The nitrogen source that most commonly limits phytoplankton growth in these waters. A pulse of nitrate into the sunlit layer is the classic precursor to a bloom. po4 mmol/m³ — phosphate The other major macronutrient. Its ratio to nitrate is more informative than either level alone — see the Redfield ratio in the features chapter. si mmol/m³ — silicate Diatoms build glass shells out of silicate; flagellates do not. When silicate runs out relative to nitrogen, the competitive advantage shifts toward the flagellates that dominate harmful blooms. o2 mmol/m³ — dissolved oxygen What fish breathe. The Arabian Sea has one of the world's most intense oxygen minimum zones, which compresses habitat vertically and is why this is a habitat feature, not just a bloom aftermath signal. nppv mg/m³/day — net primary production The rate at which carbon is being fixed by photosynthesis — the productivity of the water, as opposed to chl which is the standing stock already there. Wind and wind stress (Problem A only) Five variables from an L4 reprocessed scatterometer wind product. Wind matters because it is the forcing — the mechanism that injects nutrients into the sunlit layer and starts a bloom in the first place. eastward_stress Pa — zonal wind stress The eastward force per unit area the wind exerts on the sea surface. This is the direct driver of Ekman transport. northward_stress Pa — meridional wind stress The northward component of the same force. stress_curl Pa/m — curl of the wind stress How much the stress field rotates in space. Positive curl in the northern hemisphere pushes surface water apart and pulls deep, nutrient-rich water up — open-ocean upwelling. eastward_wind m/s — 10 m eastward wind Wind speed at 10 m above the sea. Fully populated even where the stress fields are masked, which is why it is kept alongside them. northward_wind m/s — 10 m northward wind The northward component of the 10 m wind. Why observed stress instead of ERA5 winds The classic recipe is to take 10 m winds from ERA5 and convert them to stress with a bulk formula: τ = ρ_air · C_d · |U| · U . The problem is C_d , the drag coefficient — it is treated as a constant (1.3 × 10⁻³) but in reality varies with sea state and atmospheric stability. It is the least defensible number in the calculation. This Copernicus product serves scatterometer-derived stress directly , reachable with credentials we already have, with no drag-coefficient assumption entering at all. ERA5 would have meant a second account for a strictly worse version of the same covariate. (It remains the right source for things Copernicus does not carry — precipitation, air–sea heat flux.) The coverage caveat The stress fields cover about 61% of grid cells, and the missing 39% is a fixed spatial mask , not scattered gaps — every cell is either always present or always absent. Daily averaging cannot repair that. The 10 m wind fields are fully populated, so rows without stress still carry wind speed, LightGBM handles the missing stress natively, and a data_quality column records the difference so the model can condition on it. Bathymetry NOAA's ERDDAP serves the same global relief grid GEBCO publishes, over plain HTTP with the bounding box in the URL and no account required. It returns altitude (positive up, so ocean is negative); we convert once, at ingestion, to depth in positive metres with land as NaN. depth m, positive down Seafloor depth. Ecologically enormous — the shelf break at ~200 m separates two completely different worlds — and non-linear, which is why it also enters as log-depth and as a categorical bucket. seafloor_slope m per degree How steeply the bottom drops away. Steep slopes and shelf breaks force water upward and are persistent aggregation features for fish. distance_to_coast km Great-circle distance from each ocean cell to the nearest land cell. Derived from the elevation grid (land = elevation ≥ 0) rather than from gaps in the ocean fields, so a genuine data hole over water is never mistaken for a coastline. OBIS occurrence records The Ocean Biodiversity Information System is a global aggregator of marine species occurrence records — museum specimens, research surveys, tagging programmes, citizen science. Two distinct queries are made: Target species occurrences — records of the five modelled species. These become the positive class. The target group — every occurrence record for Actinopterygii (ray-finned fishes, OBIS taxon ID 10194) in the same region and window. These are not absences; they are the pool that pseudo-absences get drawn from. Why that matters is the core of the habitat chapter . Practical details that cost real debugging time: OBIS caps a single response well below the size of these queries, so deep paging through the after cursor is mandatory — an un-paged call silently truncates. And eventDate is a heterogeneous free-text-ish field that sometimes carries ranges like 2013-02-01/2013-02-28 , so the parser takes the start of any range before parsing. Records without a usable latitude, longitude or date are dropped. Fetch engineering: three things that are load-bearing Getting these variables out of Copernicus is not a formality. Three decisions each turn a request that takes seconds into one that takes hours, or never completes. 1. Service choice: arco-time-series , never arco-geo-series Copernicus serves the same data through two Zarr services with opposite chunking. arco-geo-series stores huge latitude/longitude chunks with one timestep each — right for "the whole globe, latest snapshot", which is what map tile rendering needs. arco-time-series stores fine lat/lon chunks with huge time chunks — right for "one bounded area, many timesteps", which is exactly our access pattern. Pick the wrong one and the client effectively fetches the globe once per day of your range. The difference is seconds versus hours. 2. The depth bound must be server-side These reanalysis products carry 50 depth levels . Only the surface is ever used here. Passing minimum_depth / maximum_depth into open_dataset makes the server do the selection: ds = copernicusmarine.open_dataset( dataset_id="cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m", variables=["thetao", "so", "uo", "vo", "zos", "mlotst"], service="arco-time-series", # bounded area, many timesteps minimum_longitude=68.0, maximum_longitude=78.0, minimum_latitude=6.0, maximum_latitude=23.0, start_datetime="2016-01-01T00:00:00", end_datetime="2021-12-31T23:59:59", minimum_depth=0.0, maximum_depth=1.0, # <- surface only, server-side ) Measured, not assumed With the depth bound, one representative request takes ~63 seconds . Without it, the identical request did not complete in 15 minutes . This is specific to these 50-level reanalysis products — the near-real-time products the live map uses have a singleton depth dimension where a post-hoc isel(depth=0) is harmless. 3. Hourly products must be downsampled inside the fetch loop The only multi-year wind product is hourly. One calendar month of five variables over the Arabian Sea box is ~324 MB in memory and takes ~85 seconds. Six years fetched in one call would be ~7.8 GB held at once — to produce ~160 MB of daily means. So fetch_wind requests one calendar month, averages it to daily (skipping the swath-gap NaNs rather than letting one missing hour void the day), and only then requests the next month. Peak memory stays at one month regardless of window length. Measured fetch performance Product Request Time physics 1/12° daily 8×14° box, 30 days ~63 s physics 1/12° daily 10×17° box, 2 years ~60 s physics 1/12° monthly 40×30° box, 14 years ~76 s bgc 1/4° daily 10×17° box, 2 years ~24 s bgc 1/4° monthly 40×30° box, 14 years ~34 s wind 1/8° hourly 10×17° box, 1 month ~85 s (324 MB) A full raw-zone fetch for both problems is about 4 minutes and 840 MB on disk. Everything is cached as NetCDF with the dataset ID, region, window and cadence written into the file attributes — these products get reprocessed periodically, so the dataset ID alone is not enough to reproduce a training run. Two fetch profiles, and why they differ Problem B (habitat) Problem A (HAB) Region North Indian Ocean, 55–95°E / 5°S–25°N Arabian Sea, 68–78°E / 6–23°N Cadence Monthly Daily Window 2000–2013 2016–2021 Sources physics, BGC, bathymetry, OBIS physics, BGC, wind stress, bathymetry Constrained by label availability interannual variability Wind is HAB-only: the habitat pipeline runs on monthly means, where daily wind stress has no meaning. The fusion layer takes wind as an optional argument precisely so that omitting it changes nothing else about the resulting table.

label: The fusion layer
title: The Marine Data Fusion Layer
text: Machine learning The Marine Data Fusion Layer Raw products arrive on four different grids at four different cadences. This layer brings them onto one common grid, computes the shared derived fields, records how complete each row actually is, and hands both problems an identical view of the ocean. It is written once and imported by both. Why this exists at all Physics arrives at 1/12°, biogeochemistry at 1/4°, bathymetry at 15 arc-seconds, wind at 1/8°. If each problem's pipeline did its own regridding, "sea surface temperature gradient" would end up meaning two subtly different computations in two places — and nobody would notice until the two models disagreed for reasons no one could explain. The layer supports exactly two access shapes, because the two problems genuinely need different ones: Function Returns Used by build_gridded_frame() The full (latitude, longitude, date) cube as a tidy table — one row per cell per day. Problem A, and the prediction-raster export for the map. sample_at_points() Ocean state at scattered observation points. Problem B — occurrence records are points, not a grid, and materialising the whole cube to read a few thousand cells would be wasteful. Both paths share the same regridding and derived-field code, so a feature means the same thing whichever way it was obtained. That is train/serve parity enforced by construction rather than by discipline. The common grid Everything is interpolated onto a regular 0.25° latitude/longitude grid. That is the biogeochemistry product's native resolution — the coarsest real input — so the operation is a genuine downsample of the fine physics rather than an invented upsample of biogeochemistry. Inventing resolution you do not have is a way of manufacturing confidence you have not earned. Cell centres are snapped to exact multiples of the resolution, so two regions built at the same resolution share cell boundaries exactly. Without that, the shared feature store would not actually be shareable. Interpolation is linear, and land stays NaN — there is no interpolation across a coastline. Linear is the right choice in the downsampling direction and stays honest in the other: it will not invent structure finer than the source had. Shared derived fields Once everything is on the grid, the fields that both problems need get computed once, here, rather than twice and slightly differently in two pipelines: Field Computed from Meaning sst_gradient thetao Frontal strength — how sharply temperature changes across space. chl_gradient log(1 + chl) Chlorophyll front strength. Taken in log space, because chlorophyll spans orders of magnitude and a raw-unit gradient just tracks the local mean. current_speed uo, vo Magnitude of the surface current. okubo_weiss uo, vo Separates eddy interiors from the strain-dominated filaments between them. relative_vorticity uo, vo Sign distinguishes cyclonic from anticyclonic rotation. eddy_kinetic_energy uo, vo Energy in the flow relative to the time-mean flow at each cell. wind_stress_magnitude eastward/northward_stress Total force per unit area on the sea surface. upwelling_index observed wind stress Bakun-style coastal upwelling index. ekman_pumping stress_curl Open-ocean upwelling velocity. wind_speed eastward/northward_wind 10 m wind speed. depth bathymetry Seafloor depth, positive down. seafloor_slope depth Gradient magnitude of the depth field. distance_to_coast elevation ≥ 0 Great-circle distance to the nearest land cell. The physics behind each of these is explained in the feature engineering chapter . What matters here is when they are computed. Ordering matters, and getting it wrong is silent For the point-sampling path, derived fields are computed on the grid, before sampling — never from the sampled values afterwards. A spatial gradient or an Okubo–Weiss parameter is a property of a field's neighbourhood ; it simply cannot be recovered from an isolated point. Computing it after sampling would produce a different, wrong feature under the same name, and the two pipelines would silently disagree. Data quality as a feature, not a cleanup step Every row carries a data_quality column: the fraction of core ocean variables (thetao, so, chl, uo, vo) actually present, rather than gap-filled. This is a feature, deliberately, not something silently imputed away. A prediction standing on three gap-filled inputs should be able to say so, and the model can learn to condition its own confidence on it. Rows with no ocean variable at all are land or outside coverage, and those are dropped — keeping them would just be a hole in every downstream feature. A guard that caught a real failure mode Merging the source grids uses an inner join on time, which silently truncates to the shortest input. A half-finished wind fetch would therefore shrink the entire feature store down to the wind window — and still look like a successful build. The model would train on a fraction of the intended record with nothing to indicate it. core_steps = len(np.intersect1d(physics_grid["time"], bgc_grid["time"])) if merged.sizes["time"] < core_steps: raise FusionError( f"merging dropped {core_steps - merged.sizes['time']} of {core_steps} " "timesteps. An optional covariate (wind?) covers a shorter period than " "physics/bgc — re-fetch it for the full window, or pass wind=None." ) The reference is the physics-and-biogeochemistry overlap, which defines the ocean-state record we intend to model. An optional covariate is not allowed to shorten it. The feature store The built table is written once to Parquet and reused. Rebuilding the HAB feature table costs about 7 minutes, so caching it means re-runs go straight to training. Passing --refresh-features forces a rebuild. Memory: why every column is float32 The HAB feature table is roughly 3.9 million rows × 151 columns. At float64 that is ~4.7 GB for one copy — and scikit-learn's ColumnTransformer plus LightGBM each make more. On a 9 GB machine that is an out-of-memory kill with no traceback. So numeric columns are downcast to float32 on write and again on read. float32 carries about 7 significant digits; these are geophysical measurements good to 3–4 digits at best, so the precision lost is far below the measurement error already in the data. Peak memory went from ~9 GB to ~2.5 GB. Downcasting on read is not enough For a while the store on disk was still float64 — it predated the downcast being wired into the write path, and the read path compensated. But it compensated after read_parquet had already materialised the full-width table, so every experiment still paid the doubled peak the downcast exists to avoid. Rewriting the file once removed that permanently: Before After File on disk 2.80 GB 1.59 GB Full read, peak memory ~7 GB 2.82 GB 20-of-151-column read 3.5 s / 2.82 GB 0.1 s / 1.08 GB That last row is the one that changes day-to-day work. Parquet is columnar, so asking for 20 of 151 columns reads about 13% of the file rather than all of it — and an experiment usually wants a handful of features, not the whole matrix. Selecting columns after the read returns an identical frame while paying the full cost, which is why the projection is pushed down into Parquet and why the test asserts on what Parquet was asked for rather than on the frame that comes back. The rewrite itself streams row group by row group and casts with Arrow rather than pandas, for the obvious reason: loading 3.9M × 151 float64 values in order to downcast them would need exactly the peak being removed. Two exceptions, both deliberate Coordinates stay float64. Everything downstream groups on latitude and longitude — climatology, spatial blocks, per-cell lags. float32 rounding could make two rows of the same grid cell compare unequal and silently split one cell into two groups. Pandas nullable integer columns become float32. A single Int8 column makes ColumnTransformer fall back to object dtype for the entire concatenated matrix, which is far larger and far slower than the float32 it should be. Missing values land as NaN, which LightGBM handles natively anyway. A gotcha worth knowing about Surface-level Copernicus datasets carry a scalar depth coordinate at slightly different float precision between products — 0.494025 in one, 0.49402538 in another. xarray.merge treats that as a conflict, which broke every mixed physics + biogeochemistry request until the depth coordinate was dropped after the surface level is selected. It is the kind of bug that looks like nonsense until you print the coordinate to full precision.

label: Feature engineering
title: Feature engineering
text: Machine learning Feature engineering Twenty-two raw variables become 136 features for the bloom model and 40 for the habitat model. This chapter explains every family of them — the geometry features that encode ocean physics, the temporal features that encode history, and the problem-specific ones that encode biology — and why each was worth computing. The organising principle A raw measurement answers "what is the value here, now". Almost every question worth asking is comparative: Is this value unusual for this place, in this season ? → anomaly features Where is it heading? → difference and rolling features What happened upstream in time? → lag features Is there a boundary here? → gradient features Is the water rotating or being pulled apart? → eddy features Is deep, nutrient-rich water being pushed up? → upwelling features Everything below is one of those six shapes. And every single one of them is backward-looking by construction — the only forward shift anywhere in the codebase is the target itself. Shared: spatial geometry features These live in marine_ml/features/geometry.py and are used by both problems. They are computed on the regular grid, so spacing is in degrees — and where a physical unit matters the conversion to metres is applied explicitly. One detail that would have biased every east–west gradient A degree of longitude gets shorter as you move away from the equator. At 20°N it is about 6% shorter than at the equator. Every horizontal gradient is therefore divided by 111,320 · cos(latitude) in the east–west direction and by a constant 111,320 in the north–south direction. Skip this and every zonal gradient in the domain is systematically wrong, in a way that grows with latitude. Fronts — gradient_magnitude Jargon buster — a front An ocean front is a boundary where two water masses meet, showing up as a sharp horizontal change in temperature, salinity or colour over a short distance. Fronts matter because they physically concentrate things: nutrients get pushed up along them, plankton accumulate, small fish come to eat the plankton, and big fish come to eat the small fish. INCOIS's operational PFZ advisory is, at heart, a hand-tuned SST front detector — these features are the learned version of the same signal. |∇T| = √( (∂T/∂y / 111320)² + (∂T/∂x / (111320·cos φ))² ) T is the field (temperature or log-chlorophyll), φ is latitude. A centred difference stands in for the Sobel operator: on a smooth geophysical field at this resolution the two agree closely, and it handles irregular edges and the NaN land mask without padding gymnastics. Eddies — okubo_weiss and relative_vorticity Jargon buster — mesoscale eddies The ocean is full of rotating vortices tens to hundreds of kilometres across, called mesoscale eddies . They trap water — and whatever is in it — and carry it for weeks. Cyclonic eddies pull deep nutrient-rich water up in their centres, making them productive; many pelagic species aggregate around eddy edges rather than their centres. The Okubo–Weiss parameter separates rotation-dominated flow from strain-dominated flow: W = Sₙ² + Sₛ² − ω² Sₙ = ∂u/∂x − ∂v/∂y (normal strain) Sₛ = ∂v/∂x + ∂u/∂y (shear strain) ω = ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y (relative vorticity) W is negative where rotation beats strain — that is an eddy interior. W is positive in the stretched filaments between eddies. Units are s⁻². relative_vorticity keeps the sign separately, because in the northern hemisphere positive means cyclonic and negative anticyclonic, and those are ecologically different. eddy_kinetic_energy is computed against the time-mean flow at each cell, so a persistent boundary current does not falsely read as eddy activity. Upwelling — the mechanism behind blooms Jargon buster — Ekman transport and upwelling Wind blowing over the sea does not push the surface water in the direction it blows. The Earth's rotation deflects it — to the right in the northern hemisphere. Net water transport in the wind-driven surface layer ends up at 90° to the wind. This is Ekman transport . When that transport pushes water away from a coast, water must come from somewhere to replace it, and it comes from below: cold, dark, nutrient-rich deep water rises into the sunlit layer. That is coastal upwelling , and it is why the world's most productive fisheries sit on upwelling coasts. It is also the nutrient injection that precedes many harmful blooms. Two physically distinct mechanisms are captured, and the Arabian Sea needs both: Coastal: the Bakun upwelling index UI = τ_alongshore / (ρ_sw · f) τ_alongshore = τₓ·sin θ + τ_y·cos θ f = 2Ω·sin(latitude) (Coriolis parameter) ρ_sw = 1025 kg/m³, Ω = 7.2921×10⁻⁵ rad/s, θ is coastline orientation (0° = north–south, a fair approximation for India's west coast). Units are m³/s per metre of coastline; positive means offshore transport, i.e. upwelling-favourable. The Coriolis parameter goes to zero at the equator, which would make the index infinite there. A ±2° band around the equator is masked to NaN rather than emitting an infinity that would poison the feature everywhere downstream. Open ocean: Ekman pumping w_Ekman = curl(τ) / (ρ_sw · f) Positive wind stress curl in the northern hemisphere drives surface divergence and upwells nutrient-rich water; negative curl downwells. Units are m/s. This matters specifically here: the Findlater Jet , the low-level monsoon wind jet over the Arabian Sea, has strong curl that drives a large open-ocean upwelling region well offshore of the coastal band. Blooms out there are not explained by the coastal index at all. Both features are needed, and the model uses them differently. Distance to coast Great-circle distance from each ocean cell to the nearest land cell, in km. Computed by brute-force nearest-neighbour on the unit sphere with a KD-tree — chord distance in 3D orders identically to great-circle distance, so the nearest neighbour found is the correct one, and the chord is then converted back to arc length. At these grid sizes (10⁴–10⁵ cells) that is fast enough and avoids pulling in a geospatial dependency for one feature. Shared: temporal features These live in marine_ml/features/temporal.py . The single most important property of the whole module: nothing here may look forward in time . For a row at time t , every value computed depended only on data available at or before t . Climatology and anomalies Jargon buster — climatology A climatology is the long-run average condition: "what does this grid cell normally look like in August". An anomaly is today's value minus that normal. A standardised anomaly (or z-anomaly) divides the anomaly by the local standard deviation, giving "how many typical wobbles away from normal is this" — a number that is comparable between a calm open-ocean cell and a wildly variable coastal one. For each cell and each calendar month we compute the mean and standard deviation of chlorophyll and temperature, then derive: x_anomaly = x − mean(cell, month) x_zanomaly = x_anomaly / std(cell, month) A zero or absent standard deviation (a cell observed once in training) would produce infinity, so it is replaced with NaN rather than divided through. The z-form is what makes a threshold comparable across regimes, and it is exactly why a single global chlorophyll cutoff was rejected as a bloom definition. Monthly is the right granularity here: a per-day-of-year mean over a handful of years is mostly noise. This is fitted on training rows only fit_climatology and apply_climatology are two separate functions specifically so that fitting on the wrong rows takes deliberate effort. A climatology fitted over the full record leaks the test period's own mean into training features. Lags {column}_lag{n} — the value n days ago, per cell. HAB uses lags of 3, 7, 14 and 30 days on chlorophyll, temperature, all three nutrients, primary production, mixed layer depth, both upwelling indices and wind stress magnitude. The shift is done on the date , not on row position. A gap in a cell's time series produces NaN rather than silently pulling in whatever record happens to sit adjacent in the table — which is a genuine and very quiet source of wrong features. Lagging the upwelling indices is the entire point of having wind at all: nutrient injection precedes the bloom it feeds by days to weeks, so the concurrent value is asking the wrong question. Rolling statistics Trailing mean and standard deviation over 7-, 14- and 30-day windows, for chlorophyll, temperature, current speed, both upwelling indices and wind speed. shifted = grouped[column].shift(1) # exclude today roller = shifted.rolling(steps, min_periods=max(2, steps // 2)) frame[f"{column}_roll{window}_mean"] = roller.mean() The shift(1) before rolling is what makes the window strictly trailing. A rolling window centred on t , or one that includes t , is one of the most common ways a time-series model quietly cheats. Differences — rate of change {column}_delta (first difference) and {column}_accel (second difference), for chlorophyll and temperature. A bloom is a trajectory, not a level: chlorophyll climbing steeply off a low base is a developing bloom; the same value while flat is not. Cyclical time encoding Feeding the model "day 365" and "day 1" as raw integers puts an artificial cliff between 31 December and 1 January — exactly the wrong inductive bias for a strongly seasonal system. So day-of-year and month are encoded as sine/cosine pairs, which wrap smoothly: doy_sin = sin(2π · dayofyear / 366) doy_cos = cos(2π · dayofyear / 366) month_sin = sin(2π · (month−1) / 12) month_cos = cos(2π · (month−1) / 12) 366 rather than 365 keeps leap years on the same circle instead of overshooting 2π. Monsoon phase A categorical feature, because the northern Indian Ocean's productivity cycle is monsoon-driven and its phases are qualitatively different states, not points on a smooth curve: Phase Months Regime southwest_monsoon Jun–Sep Strong upwelling-favourable winds; the main bloom season. post_monsoon Oct–Nov Winds relax, stratification rebuilds. northeast_monsoon Dec–Feb Convective mixing brings nutrients up from below — a different mechanism entirely. pre_monsoon Mar–May Warm, stratified, generally low productivity. Problem A: HAB-specific features Nutrient ratios Jargon buster — the Redfield ratio Marine plankton have a remarkably consistent elemental composition, roughly 106 carbon : 16 nitrogen : 1 phosphorus — the Redfield ratio . Departures from it tell you which nutrient is limiting growth, and therefore which kind of plankton is favoured. We compute N:P and N:Si, plus their departures from Redfield stoichiometry: n_to_p = no3 / po4 n_to_p_anomaly = n_to_p − 16 n_to_si = no3 / si n_to_si_anomaly = n_to_si − 1 Both denominators are guarded (values ≤ 1e-6 become NaN). Phosphate goes to near-zero in depleted surface water, and an unguarded ratio would produce infinities exactly where the signal is most interesting. The N:Si ratio carries information the raw concentrations do not: diatoms need silicate to build their shells, flagellates do not. Silicate depletion relative to nitrogen shifts the competitive advantage from diatoms toward the flagellates that dominate harmful blooms. Stratification Jargon buster — stratification and the mixed layer The mixed layer is the surface layer that wind and waves keep well stirred, so it has near-uniform temperature and density. Below it, water is denser and does not readily mix upward. When the mixed layer is shallow the water column is strongly stratified . For a bloom this is decisive. Phytoplankton need light, which only exists near the surface. A shallow mixed layer keeps them there; a deep one keeps mixing them down into the dark where they cannot grow. stratification_index = 1 / (1 + mlotst) log_mld = log(1 + mlotst) warm_shallow_index = thetao / (1 + mlotst) warm_shallow_index is an interaction term: warm water over a shallow mixed layer is the strongest bloom-retention signal, and neither term expresses it alone. Upwelling interactions upwelling_x_stratification — upwelling only injects nutrients into the sunlit zone where the water column is shallow enough for the pumped water to reach it, so the interaction carries more signal than either term alone. upwelling_favourable — the index clipped at zero. Downwelling is a different regime rather than "negative upwelling", and separating them lets the model treat them as such. Marine heatwave flag Following the Hobday definition: sea surface temperature above the local seasonal 90th percentile for at least 5 consecutive days . The duration requirement is the part that matters — a single warm day is weather; five consecutive is an event with ecological consequences. Implemented in standardised-anomaly space, which keeps the threshold local and seasonal without fitting a separate percentile surface: the z-score cutting off the 90th percentile of a standard normal is 1.2816. Run lengths are computed per cell with a cumulative-count trick, and both the binary flag and the current hot_run_length are kept. What gets excluded from the HAB model's inputs Excluded Why bloom_t3 / bloom_t5 / bloom_t7 These are the answers. chl_t3 / chl_t5 / chl_t7 Future chlorophyll — the quantity being forecast. threshold_t* The future threshold used to build the label. threshold , bloom_exceedance Derived from the label definition itself. latitude , longitude , date , season , region Raw identifiers, not physics. Note what stays in : chl itself and is_bloom at time t . The current chlorophyll level is legitimate input to forecasting the future level, and whether it is blooming now is fair game as a feature — it is blooming at t+h that is the answer. But threshold and bloom_exceedance are derived from the label definition, so they go. Problem B: habitat-specific features Prey-availability lag Chlorophyll 30 and 60 days earlier, not concurrent. A phytoplankton bloom takes weeks to propagate up the food chain to anything a fishing vessel would target — asking "is there chlorophyll here today" is the wrong question. Implemented by re-sampling the same fields at a shifted date rather than by shifting rows, because these are scattered points with irregular dates and there is no per-cell time series to shift along. chl_trend_30d (current minus 30-day-ago) captures whether the prey base was building or collapsing, not just its level. Thermal niche Every species has a temperature range it is actually found in. We fit that range per species, from training presences only , and then place each row's local temperature within it: thermal_low = 5th percentile of temperature at this species' presences thermal_high = 95th percentile thermal_optimum = median thermal_position = (T − thermal_low) / (thermal_high − thermal_low) thermal_distance = |T − thermal_optimum| in_thermal_range = thermal_low ≤ T ≤ thermal_high thermal_position outside 0–1 means the location is outside the species' observed thermal range. The niche is refitted inside every cross-validation fold — fitting it once outside the loop would leak held-out temperatures into a training feature. Bathymetric context Depth spans four orders of magnitude and its ecological effect is strongly non-linear near the shelf break, so depth enters three ways: raw, as log_depth , and as a categorical bucket a linear baseline could never discover on its own. Bucket Depth range nearshore < 50 m shelf 50 – 200 m slope 200 – 1,000 m deep 1,000 – 3,000 m abyssal > 3,000 m Species identity as a feature species_key is a categorical input, one-hot encoded. That is what makes this one model rather than five, and it is the tabular analogue of a shared encoder with species-specific output heads — species with few records borrow strength from the shared environmental response. Latitude and longitude are deliberately excluded With spatially clustered presences, a tree model will happily memorise "presence lives at 12.3°N, 74.8°E" and score beautifully under random cross-validation while learning no ecology whatsoever. Spatial structure has to enter through environment and bathymetry instead. This is the difference between a model that has learned where fish live and one that has learned a map. A bug worth reading about: the feature list that depended on call order The habitat model originally scored much lower (cross-validated TSS 0.66, holdout 0.53). The cause: feature_columns() discovered its column list by inspecting the table, and it was called before apply_thermal_niche had added the thermal columns. Meanwhile species_key sat in the excluded-identifier set. The result was a model with no species-dependent input at all . Five "species" were one pooled model wearing five labels, and the carefully per-fold-fitted thermal niche was computed and then thrown away. It was found by checking whether the exported per-species map tiles actually differed. They were byte-identical. The fix was to name those columns explicitly ( THERMAL_FEATURES , SPECIES_FEATURE ) so that the feature list cannot depend on the order two functions happen to be called in. Holdout TSS went from 0.53 to 0.788.

label: Problem A — HAB
title: HAB early warning
text: Problem A HAB early warning: labels, model, results Forecasting harmful algal blooms three, five and seven days ahead across the Arabian Sea: how the labels are constructed, what the model is, how it is validated against a deliberately strong baseline, why its probabilities need calibrating, and what it actually scores. Building the labels Nobody hands you a column that says "bloom". It has to be constructed, in three steps, and the order matters enormously. Step 1 — fit a threshold, on training rows only For each grid cell and each monsoon season, take the 90th percentile of chlorophyll observed there during the training period. That is the bloom threshold for that cell in that season. Two fallbacks handle sparse groups: Fewer than 24 observations in a (cell, season) group → fall back to that cell's all-season threshold. Still nothing → fall back to a single global threshold. A percentile estimated from a handful of points is noise, and would define blooms in places they never occur. Step 2 — apply it everywhere Every row gets is_bloom (is chlorophyll ≥ threshold right now) and bloom_exceedance (how far above the local normal — the severity signal). Rows with missing chlorophyll get a missing label rather than a false zero. Step 3 — shift forward to make the target for horizon in (3, 5, 7): chl_t{h} = grouped["chl"].shift(-horizon) # future chlorophyll threshold_t{h} = grouped["threshold"].shift(-horizon) # its threshold bloom_t{h} = chl_t{h} >= threshold_t{h} This is the only forward shift in the entire codebase And it is correct here, because it constructs the target , not a feature. It is deliberately isolated in labels.py so that auditing "does anything in this project read the future" is a single-file question. The tests enforce that everything in the temporal feature library is trailing by construction. What the label rate actually is Period Bloom rate at t+7 Train (2016 → mid-2020) 10.2% Validation 9.4% Test (2021) 7.6% Flat across periods, which is what you want — the thresholds are fitted on training years only, so drift in the label rate would mean the model is being scored on a differently-defined target than it was trained on. On the earlier two-year window this went 10.4% → 16.5% → 21.2%, and that drift was destroying the model. The model One LightGBM classifier per horizon, inside a scikit-learn pipeline that casts numeric columns to float32 and one-hot encodes the two categorical features (monsoon phase and depth bucket). Hyperparameter Value Reasoning n_estimators 500 With a learning rate of 0.05, enough rounds to fit without needing early stopping machinery. learning_rate 0.05 Conservative. Each tree contributes little, so the sum is stable. num_leaves 31 LightGBM default; paired with a depth cap so trees stay shallow. max_depth 6 Hard cap on interaction order. Deeper trees memorise the training years. min_child_samples 50 No leaf may be built from fewer than 50 rows — prevents splits on noise. subsample / colsample 0.8 / 0.8 Row and column sampling per tree; standard variance reduction. reg_lambda 1.0 L2 penalty on leaf weights. class_weight balanced Blooms are ~8% of rows. Without reweighting the model learns to always say no. Hand-chosen and deliberately conservative. There is no hyperparameter search — nested rolling-origin tuning is the documented next step, and an un-nested search would just be another way to leak the test period. Training stride: fitting on every 4th day Consecutive daily fields in this basin are nearly identical — the same autocorrelation that makes persistence a strong baseline. So the effective sample size is far below the row count, and fitting on every 4th calendar day discards little information while cutting fit time and memory proportionally. Whole days are dropped, never individual cells, so every retained timestep is still a complete spatial field. Training still sees ~550 days spread across six years and all six monsoon cycles. Fitting only The stride applies to model fitting. Evaluation always uses every row of the test period — subsampling what you score on would be a different and much less defensible thing to do. Validation: rolling-origin CV with an embargo Each fold trains on everything before a cutoff and tests on the window after it, with horizon days dropped in between. fold 1: [========== train ==========] x [== test ==] fold 2: [============== train ==============] x [== test ==] fold 3: [================== train ==================] x [== test ==] ↑ embargo gap The gap is not fussiness. The label at time t is chlorophyll at t+7 , so a training row within 7 days of the test window shares its target's observation period. Without the gap the model is partly scored on data it was trained on, and the metric is fiction. The persistence baseline, scored on every fold Jargon buster — a persistence baseline For an autocorrelated field, "whatever is happening now will still be happening later" is a genuinely strong forecast. In weather forecasting this is the standard sanity check. Persistence here means: it is blooming now, therefore it will be blooming at t+h. Any model that cannot beat persistence has demonstrated nothing, no matter how good its absolute score looks. Our baseline uses the standardised chlorophyll anomaly squashed through a sigmoid rather than a bare 0/1, so it is a ranked score — otherwise ranking metrics would penalise it unfairly for ties. The baseline earned its place immediately On the first (2020–2021) run, the model lost to persistence at t+5 and t+7. That finding is invisible without the baseline — the raw PR-AUC looked respectable. It is what drove the window out to six years. Calibration: making the probability mean something class_weight="balanced" deliberately distorts the decision boundary to keep the minority class learnable. The side effect is systematic overconfidence : the raw model's 0.9–1.0 prediction bin actually fires on only 57% of occasions. Ranking metrics do not care — PR-AUC and TSS only look at the ordering. But the product surfaces a probability to a coastal agency, and "70% chance of a bloom" has to mean something. The fix is isotonic regression : fit a monotonic step function mapping raw scores onto observed frequencies. Where it is fitted is the entire question: Slice Can it be the calibration set? Why Training No The model is near-perfect there, so the mapping learned would be roughly the identity. Validation Yes Unseen by the model, and not used for the final score. Test No That would be fitting on the data you are about to report. This is why the validation slice is no longer folded back into training for the final fit — having something honest to calibrate on is worth more than the extra three months of training data. Isotonic regression is monotonic, so PR-AUC and ROC-AUC are unchanged to three decimals by construction. The improvement shows up exactly where it should — in the Brier score: Horizon Brier (raw) Brier (calibrated) Improvement t+3 0.056 0.038 32% t+5 0.073 0.049 32% t+7 0.085 0.057 33% Results Held-out final period: 2021, 577,608 grid-cell-days, 7.3–7.6% bloom rate. This period was touched exactly once, at the end. Horizon PR-AUC Persistence ROC-AUC TSS Brier t+3 0.661 0.511 0.942 0.751 0.038 t+5 0.493 0.384 0.884 0.635 0.049 t+7 0.362 0.309 0.841 0.564 0.057 The model beats persistence at every horizon. Rolling-origin cross-validation agrees at every horizon too (t+7: 0.363 CV vs 0.362 holdout), which is the sign that the holdout number is not a fluke of one lucky period. The number that decides deployability PR-AUC is a summary across all thresholds. An operational system runs at one threshold, and it is chosen by the recall a coastal agency demands — missing a bloom costs far more than a false alarm. Set the threshold to catch 80% of blooms and this is what you get: Horizon Precision Recall False-alarm rate t+3 0.449 0.807 0.551 t+5 0.280 0.801 0.720 t+7 0.202 0.811 0.798 Read the false-alarm column before treating t+7 as deployable Catching 80% of blooms a week out means four in five alerts are false . No coastal agency will keep acting on that; operator trust erodes and then the true alerts get ignored too. The t+3 alert, where roughly half of alerts are genuine, is the one that would survive contact with a real agency. That is a more useful conclusion than any AUC on this page. What the model actually uses Mean absolute SHAP value — how much each feature moves predictions on average — at t+3: Rank Feature Mean |SHAP| What it is 1 chl_anomaly 0.573 Chlorophyll minus this cell's seasonal normal. 2 chl_zanomaly 0.551 The same, standardised by local variability. 3 chl 0.480 Current chlorophyll level. 4 is_bloom 0.470 Is it blooming right now. 5 chl_delta 0.355 Day-over-day change — the growth rate. 6 chl_gradient 0.291 Spatial sharpness of the chlorophyll field. 7 doy_cos 0.259 Season. 8 po4 0.200 Phosphate. 9 chl_accel 0.192 Is the growth rate itself accelerating. 13 upwelling_index_roll30_std 0.096 Variability of upwelling over the past 30 days. At t+7 the split of total |SHAP| is chlorophyll and its 18 derivatives 36.8% against 14.4% for all 41 wind-derived features combined . Wind is a real but secondary contributor. A sanity check that passed The highest-ranked upwelling features at t+7 are the 30-day rolling statistics — upwelling_index_roll30_std at rank 16 and upwelling_index_roll30_mean at rank 28 — rather than any instantaneous value. That is the physically expected shape: sustained upwelling over weeks drives nutrient supply, not one windy day. When a feature ranks the way the physics predicts it should, that is mild evidence it is measuring what it claims to. The earlier, higher, worse numbers An earlier 2020–2021 run reported t+3 0.755 / t+5 0.525 / t+7 0.468 — higher absolute numbers that were worse models . Two compounding problems: 1. It lost to persistence at t+5 and t+7 (0.548 and 0.492). Invisible without the baseline. 2. Even those figures were propped up by an evaluation artifact. They came from fitting on train + validation, i.e. right up to the test boundary. Moving the validation slice out of training — necessary to have anything to calibrate on — collapsed the model: Training window PR-AUC ROC-AUC TSS train + val, ends Sep 2021 0.468 0.764 0.389 train only, ends May 2021 0.235 0.531 0.064 ROC-AUC 0.53 is chance. A 3.5-month gap between the end of training and the start of testing destroyed it. On six years of data the same honest gap gives 0.841. The lesson worth keeping The current numbers are lower and far more trustworthy. Absolute metric values are not comparable across evaluation setups, and a rising number can mean a leakier evaluation rather than a better model . If your score jumps after a change, the first question is what the change did to the split, not whether to celebrate. Caveats that still stand Weak labels. Everything here trains on modelled chlorophyll above a percentile. Verified in-situ blooms would be far rarer, and the whole class-imbalance strategy would need revisiting with them.
